speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We have a duty not just to ensure the strength of our services that cater to the public, but to make the access to such services, easy, prompt and making as few demands as possible on the time and attention of the Singaporeans we serve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The second is how we want decisions to be made for us when we no longer have the mental capacity to make them ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The first set of amendments are to facilitate the work of various agencies involved in the conveyancing process, led by the Singapore Land Authority (SLA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The second set of amendments are proposed by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will start by first focusing on the amendments relating to property conveyancing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Property conveyancing is the legal process of transferring the title in a property from one party to another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore has a robust property conveyancing framework, which provides a foundation for stable and reliable property rights and in turn, gives certainty to individuals and businesses alike in their dealings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, anyone who has gone through the process will know that it is largely manual and paper-based.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in part due to the lack of a fully digital platform and existing legal requirements for conveyancing transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, legislation today requires that contracts for sale of immovable property and deeds of conveyance of immovable property must be in writing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Wet-ink signatures for those documents, which, in turn, necessitate physical meetings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, payments are primarily made through cashier's orders that must be purchased and delivered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Physical documentation is, therefore, still integral to the property transaction process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And considerable time is spent preparing, checking, physically delivering and safekeeping these documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We understand that such requirements can be a source of frustration to members of the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, in October 2022, a member of public wrote to Minister Josephine Teo, who was then the Minister for Communications and Information, to share his views on what he believed were some anachronistic situations, including having to arrange to make two conveyancing-related payments by cheques.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This individual questioned why digital transfers could not be supported, highlighting the inconvenience this posed for individuals, like himself, who had no cheque book.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: He also highlighted that even the process of opening an account for the purposes of a new cheque book was so tedious that his bank advised that it would be easier for him to borrow someone else's cheque book instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our agencies have been aware of these issues and have been working hard, over the years, to electronise the conveyancing process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The DCP, which is a fully electronic end-to-end conveyancing platform for property transactions, was first announced at the Committee of Supply (COS) debate in 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I had also provided an update in March at the COS debate earlier this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With the DCP in development, we have been able to reassure members of public, such as the individual I mentioned earlier, of our plans to digitalise the conveyancing process, while we carefully continue the development of the DCP, taking the necessary time to account for the scale and complexities involved in digitalising the entire conveyancing process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: During this time, SLA has also worked with key stakeholders, such as the Council for Estate Agencies (CEA), the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA), the Central Provident Fund Board (CPFB), the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), the Housing and Development Board (HDB), the Singapore Academy of Law, the Law Society of Singapore, the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS), the Association of Banks in Singapore, banks and financial institutions, to ensure their perspectives have been considered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some of the features of the DCP will include, a streamlined and user-friendly experience, with guided workflows and online transaction milestones to help parties navigate the conveyancing process; robust authentication and verification measures to enable parties to sign electronic contracts for sale of immovable property securely; tools that enable seamless communication, coordination and tracking between lawyers, financial institutions, real estate firms, agents and government agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When fully implemented, DCP will thus provide increased efficiency, greater convenience, improved coordination and tracking as well as enhanced transparency and security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will help to address some of the pain points and feedback which have been raised to us, including those that I had mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, facilitating electronic transfers of conveyancing monies will mean buyers no longer have to spend time and effort applying for cheque books which they may otherwise not need, while solicitors no longer need to arrange for physical trips to the bank to arrange for payments to be made by cashier's order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Property agents can also better track the progress of the property transactions under their charge through the DCP instead of manually checking in with the seller or buyer, or their solicitors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Solicitors and clients can also save time and effort by applying digital signatures in a secured platform as opposed to making arrangements for wet-ink signatures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: SLA has been providing extensive support to parties that wish to start transacting over the DCP, with 14 training workshops held for 28 law firms, 67 lawyers and 112 conveyancing executives who will be participating in the pilot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, an estimated 38% of law firms by market share have been onboarded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: New functionalities will be added in each phase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The DCP will also expand the types of property transactions – private residential, commercial and industrial property transactions – in phases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Another enabler in the digitalisation of the conveyancing process is the HDB Flat Portal, which covers the processes relating to the sale and purchase of HDB flats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Launched in January 2021, this integrated online portal streamlines the process of buying and selling HDB flats through features, such as the customised financial calculators, HDB Flat Eligibility letter applications, integrated loan application service and flat listing services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the portal already enables HDB to digitalise the processing and approval of resale flat applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It will be enhanced progressively with more features, such as the use of digital signatures for signing of documents for HDB transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where HDB is appointed to act in the conveyance of an HDB flat, the portal will also enable parties to conduct flat transactions through the use of secure electronic records and electronic payments of conveyancing monies, which will be developed in tandem with DCP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the flat's transaction involves private lawyers, the portal will interface with DCP to enable data transmission and cross-platform conveyancing functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For conveyancing transactions to be carried out electronically on the DCP and the HDB Flat Portal, existing laws must be updated to create the legal framework for digital conveyancing transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The first set of amendments involve the Electronic Transactions Act 2010 (or ETA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The First Schedule to the ETA will also be amended so that Part 2 of the ETA, which contains the enabling legal framework for electronic records, electronic signatures and electronic contracts, will apply to contracts for the sale or other disposition of immovable property, disposition of an equitable interest with respect to immovable property and conveyances of immovable property executed in a PETS mentioned in sections 16U, 16V and 16W.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new Part 2B, containing new sections 16T to 16Y, will also provide a framework that will allow contracts and deeds executed electronically through the PETS to meet certain legal form requirements needed for legal validity of equivalent documents executed in writing today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new section 16U will enable a requirement under the law, including section 6(d) of the Civil Law Act 1909, that contracts for the sale or other disposition of immovable property are to be in writing and signed, to be met by a secure electronic record signed with a prescribed secure electronic signature in a PETS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new section 16V similarly enables a requirement under the law, including in section 7(2) of the Civil Law Act 1909, that a disposition of an equitable interest respecting any immovable property or interest in such property is to be in writing and signed, to be met by a secure electronic record signed with a prescribed secure electronic signature in a PETS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new section 16W will enable deeds for the conveyance or transfer of any estate or interest in immovable property and deeds of security for payment of monies under a mortgage to be electronically executed validly in PETS if conditions in new section 16W(3) are met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Section 16X only applies to the witnessing of the execution of a conveyancing document in a PETS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, the technology used to enable the witnessing must fulfil certain technical requirements, and witnesses and signatories must both be in Singapore at the time of the remote witnessing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Deeds which are executed physically today must meet common law legal formalities and requirements that include being in writing on paper or parchment, being sealed and being delivered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As part of the new section, 16W(3) introduces requirements that must be satisfied in order for an electronic record to meet the requirements of a deed under a rule of law that requires a conveyance or transfer of immovable property or an instrument to secure moneys payable under a mortgage to be in the form of a deed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the electronic record must be a secure electronic record that is generated, communicated or received, and stored, in a PETS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It must also be delivered by the person executing it via the PETS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that such electronic deeds can benefit from the enhanced security mechanisms that PETS afford.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the DCP is designed such that parties may only sign using "Sign with Singpass".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the deed is being executed by a body corporate, apart from the electronic record being required to be signed by its representative or representatives in the PETS using a secure electronic signature, the new section 16W(3)(e) provides two alternative approaches in respect of the requirement to affix the common seal of the body corporate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such an electronic seal will enable a recipient of an electronic deed to more easily verify the authenticity of the electronic deed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Alternatively, the body corporate may execute the deed in accordance with other statutory requirements in lieu of sealing as provided for under other relevant written law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, where the body corporate is a company, it may execute the deed without affixing a common seal in accordance with sections 41B and 41C of the Companies Act 1967, which set out the regime for the execution of deeds without a company seal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the body corporate is a limited liability partnership, it may execute the deed in accordance with sections 7 and 8 of the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2005, which set out a regime that is similar to the one under the Companies Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In determining these requirements, we considered different factors, such as the technological tools available today, user experience and developments in other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We also took in feedback from the conveyancing community, including the Conveyancing Practice Committee of the Law Society of Singapore and we are indebted to all these partners for their feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, there is no requirement for an electronic version of a seal for deeds executed by individuals via the PETS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This takes into account that an individual executing a deed in a PETS would already be subject to enhanced authentication mechanisms, which serve a cautionary function to the individual about the nature of the instrument being executed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The individual would be required to sign the deed using a secure electronic signature in PETS, in the presence of a witness who attests the execution by the individual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A similar approach is already adopted in other settings in Singapore, where deeds executed electronically for LPA under the Mental Capacity Act 2008 are recognised as deeds without the need for seals, while the insertion of sections 41B and 41C into the Companies Act 1967 in 2017 enabled Singapore companies to dispense with affixing a company seal when executing deeds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This approach is similar with the requirements in other jurisdictions, such as the United Kingdom (UK), which has replaced the sealing requirement for deeds with other similar alternative measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Industry feedback from consultations conducted by SLA have also been supportive of adopting this position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Part 2 of the ETA contains the enabling legal framework for electronic records, electronic signatures and electronic contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Previously, these provisions did not apply to contracts for the sale or other disposition of immovable property, dispositions of an equitable interest respecting immovable property, conveyances of immovable property and instruments by deed to secure payments of monies under a mortgage, due to the inadequacy of technological infrastructure and safeguards to ensure the security and integrity of electronic property transactions at that time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, with the development of the DCP and the HDB Flat Portal, we now have the confidence in the infrastructure that will be put in place to support electronic property transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The insertion of the necessary enabling legal framework in the new Part 2B of the ETA now makes it possible to extend the application of Part 2 of the ETA to such conveyancing-related documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new provisions also provide for the prescription of requirements for the use of DCP, certain processes, evidentiary provisions as well as the processes for the correction of certain types of errors in the records of DCP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There will also be appropriate liability protection for the SLA for any loss or damage by any person arising from the person using the DCP in an improper manner, or arising from any malfunction or any cybersecurity incident, if SLA had acted in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similar amendments will be made to the Housing and Development Act 1959, to enable HDB to operate its HDB Flat Portal for public housing transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Housing and Development Act will also be amended to provide for HDB's execution of electronic deeds using an electronic seal of the Board, instead of a physical common seal, where it is required or permitted under law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: An instance of such a law is the new section 16W(3)(e)(i) of the ETA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, I will touch on the portion of the Bill that will introduce amendments to the Mental Capacity Act, which is overseen by my colleagues from MSF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These amendments are being introduced to increase the convenience of making an LPA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The LPA is a legal instrument through which a person, called a "donor", appoints one or more persons, called "donees", to make decisions on the donor's personal welfare and/or property and affairs, should the donor lose mental capacity to make such decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The execution of an instrument conferring powers of the kind in an LPA has to be witnessed in-person by a Certificate Issuer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2021, the Mental Capacity Act was amended to require as a default that an instrument to be registered as an LPA must be executed electronically and electronically submitted for registration with the Public Guardian via the Office of the Public Guardian Online (OPGO).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Although this is a default rule, the Public Guardian may make an exception if the instrument cannot be executed on the Public Guardian's electronic transaction system, such as for donors who are unable to make or sign the instrument electronically due to a physical disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today, more than 95% of LPAs are submitted digitally via the OPGO.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2021 also included a provision enabling the remote witnessing of execution of an LPA by certain donors, specifically where the Public Guardian is satisfied that there is a good reason why the donor cannot appear physically before a Certificate Issuer to execute his instrument to be registered as an LPA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This amendment has not been commenced as we now intend to avail remote witnessing to a wider segment of donors with low-risk LPA applications, provided certain legislated criteria are met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, the Public Guardian must be satisfied that none of the following risks are significant: (a) that fraud or undue pressure is used to induce the donor to execute the instrument or to execute the instrument to appoint a particular person as the donee; (b) that the donor lacks capacity to execute the instrument; and (c) that any of the proposed donees will not act in the donor's best interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Donors who do not fulfil the eligibility criteria will need to have the execution of their instrument witnessed in-person by a Certificate Issuer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will also put in place robust safeguards to minimise the risk of potential fraud or abuse during the remote witnessing process, including requiring the Certificate Issuer to declare that he had maintained proper records of the session and will be able to furnish the information to facilitate any future investigations, if needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Certificate Issuers also retain the full discretion not to proceed with certifying the donor's understanding of the purpose and scope of LPA, and that there is no fraud or undue pressure being used to induce the donor to create an LPA, should they have any concerns that the donor has lost his mental capacity or is subject to fraud or undue pressure during the remote witnessing session.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This means that the conditions that must be fulfilled for remote witnessing to satisfy any legal witnessing requirements will be consistent across the Mental Capacity Act and ETA, including the requirement that the witness and signatory must both be in Singapore at the time of remote witnessing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Through DCP and the HDB Flat Portal, property transactions will be transformed significantly from a paper-based process to a secure digital journey that benefits all Singaporeans selling and buying properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The legislative amendments have been carefully considered with security and integrity at their core.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PETS will incorporate strong and secure safeguards and measures that will ensure that the integrity of property transactions remain uncompromised as we move into the digital age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill will also enable a larger number of donors to benefit from the convenience of remote witnessing of the execution of instruments to be registered as LPAs, while ensuring sufficient safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill brings greater convenience and efficiency while maintaining the strong foundations of our property transaction system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also enhances the ease and convenience of making LPAs and, by so doing, encourages LPA adoption so as to protect the dignity and interests of Singaporeans, who may lose mental capacity later in life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If hon Members have queries on the HDB Portal and MND-related issues, Senior Minister of State Sun Xueling will respond and for LPA and MSF-related issues, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua will take these queries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It provides users the option to deal electronically with the sale of property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Other jurisdictions such as England and Australia have also moved to permit electronic conveyancing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, the typical process for selling a property involves the sellers issuing an option to the purchaser in exchange for the payment of an option fee, usually 1% of the value of the property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This option must then be exercised by payment of an option fee, usually a further 9% of the price of the property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Once the option is exercised, the purchaser then has an interest in the property and the seller is under an obligation to complete the sale in exchange for payment by the purchaser of the remaining amount of the price.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, all these processes take place with the exchange of paper documents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The options are issued in writing in paper.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Payment to exercise the option is made either by cashier’s order or cheque, usually to the seller’s designated lawyers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thereafter, if the purchaser is getting a loan or using CPF, the purchaser’s lawyers have to deal with the sellers lawyers, CPF Board and the bank and ensure that payments from all these parties along with the seller are ready for execution at the designated time for completion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, in property transactions, time is of the essence, and if any deadline for payment is missed, that will give the other party a right not to proceed with a sale and even ask for damages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In a fast moving property market, this can lead to significant claims against any party responsible for missing a deadline including purchaser, seller, lawyers, especially if a transaction does not go through.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I envisage this Bill will be a valuable service that will align with the movement of the financial industry away from paper transactions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do have a few suggestions in relation to this Bill and the electronic conveyancing process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, I note that the operative mechanism here is that any transaction in the electronic transaction mechanism will now satisfy the requirements of section 6(d) of the Civil Law Act for a transfer of property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means that this rule is not intended to replace, but rather to supplement the existing methods of conveying property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will mean a slightly more cumbersome process for parties in the industry as it means they still need to be familiar with the old processes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is sensible to have both systems operating concurrently for a transitional period, but if the Government’s intention is to transition all transactions electronically, which I think is sensible, I would suggest this be telegraphed to the market and nudges be put in place to encourage more people to transact electronically in this transition process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, where there are mistakes in the form or omissions, for example, if a selling party does not indicate the address of its conveyancing solicitor or indicates an incorrect address, under the law currently, as long as a buyer does everything in his power to indicate his intention to exercise the option, the court would generally uphold the transaction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to paper options, sometimes the exercising solicitor’s name is even left blank.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it will be important for the electronic transaction system to also have some flexibility for parties to record their exercise of the option or intention to make completion payments, even if for some reason the seller may have made some mistakes in the electronic forms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Disputes have traditionally arisen around whether the formalities for exercise of the option were met where a seller may wish to avoid a transaction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, the Land Register is generally taken as an authoritative record for the legal owner of a property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, in a fast moving market, unscrupulous sellers may sometimes issue options to more than one buyer – a practice that has been the subject of several reported court decisions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In these situations, the first party to exercise and register his or her interest in the Land Register, would generally prevail over those who register later.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One suggestion would be to see if this electronic transaction system can be linked to the Land Register such that if an option were issued in relation to the property, this may be automatically be reflected on the Land Register without the need to lodge a caveat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All my suggestions are aimed at the future of electronic transaction system.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this is an important improvement and I thank the Ministry and SLA for this initiative, which should make the conveyancing process simpler for everyone transacting in property.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the electronic facilitation of the LPA process, this is also to be welcomed and generally, I agree that any process that makes it easy for parties to enter into an LPA, the better it is.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Before I begin, I would like to declare my interest as a lawyer in private practice who has witnessed and certified LPAs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I also conduct legal clinics on LPAs as part of my grassroots work.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Currently, it is a requirement for the person giving powers under the LPA, called the donor, to be in the physical presence of the Certificate Issuer.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This Certificate Issuer must directly witness the donor using his Singpass credentials to digitally sign the document.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The donor does not have to be in the same place as the Certificate Issuer to sign the document so long as two-way visual communication is maintained, such as through an online meeting application.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate how remote signing is convenient if the donor and the Certificate Issuer cannot meet in person.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This would especially help donors who have mobility difficulties, or perhaps live too far from the Certificate Issuer.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For a start, anyone who wishes to take advantage of the remote signing option will need to apply to the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG).

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The OPG will then consider each application on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To qualify to make an application, the Bill stipulates certain conditions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While I support the Bill in its intentions to make it easier to assist donors who are immobile, I wish to raise some concerns when the LPAs involve donees who are family members.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It bears remembering that LPAs involve a substantial transfer of autonomy and are often done by older people.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The donor is authorising a close relative to have lasting power over their personal property and also, to make personal or medical decisions, when the donor’s mental capacity is lost.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There is thus always the risk that the donor's assets could be depleted by someone whom the donor is physically and emotionally dependent on.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For cases involving family members, it is straightforward to determine if the donor is under 75 years old and whether the proposed donees fall within certain categories of family relationships.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, any assessment about the risks is necessarily more subjective in nature.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: How does the OPG determine that there is no significant risk or fraud or undue pressure, and no significant risk that the proposed donees will not act in the donor’s best interest?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Practically speaking, given the workload and resources of the OPG today, does the OPG have the capacity to carefully conduct case-by-case enquiries into the family circumstances?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Or would it be the case that the application process would be largely pro-forma – that so long as the documents are in order, the approval for remote signing would generally be granted?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In other words, how would the OPG be able to properly determine that there is no significant risk that an intended LPA will be to the donor’s detriment?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It would be beneficial to get some clarity about what we can expect from the OPG in terms of specific measures and procedures.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, remote signing can also place the Certificate Issuer at a disadvantage in discharging his or her duty.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The fact that the categories of Certificate Issuers involve people with medical or legal training suggests that a Certificate Issuer has to be more than a mere rubber stamp.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Rather, there seems to be an implied responsibility for the Certificate Issuer to assess the competency and fitness of the donor to make an LPA.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In my own experience of certifying LPAs, I have found it helpful to not only pay attention to what the donor informs me, but to also observe the dynamics between the donor and donee, through their demeanour and body language.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If I believe that the donor is not able to speak freely, or the donor appears anxious or flustered, I have the option of speaking with the donor alone to confirm that the donor is not under any undue external pressure.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In the case of remote signing, however, the Certificate Issuer does not have the assurance of being able to talk with the donor alone or even verifying that there is nobody hovering around the donor.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In all likelihood, the donee might even be sitting beside the donor to guide them through the remote signing, since the donor might not be tech-savvy to do it alone.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Of course, these risks can also be present with an in-person signing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In an unfortunate scenario, any misuse of funds may go undetected for years.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: On another note, Sir, I wonder if the OPG expects a high take-up rate for remote signing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Considering that the new law will still require both the donor and the Certificate Issuer to be in Singapore, it might still be much easier and faster to arrange an in-person signing, rather than making an application for remote signing and waiting for the OPG’s approval to proceed.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If the concern is to make the LPA procedures more convenient and accessible to donors, might I suggest the option of introducing more categories of Certificate Issuers be considered?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In the UK, registered social workers can witness and certify LPAs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that many of our social workers have a heavy workload.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But there may be some who may be interested to be Certificate Issuers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps the Government can open the option for them to receive training and accreditation from the OPG?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Another option is to hold more legal clinics and roadshows on LPAs in the neighborhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I understand this has been ongoing in many constituencies and should continue.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In Malay, Sir. :   Sir, one last point.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In the previous Sitting, I filed a question about the demographic breakdown of LPA donors.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: MUIS can also collaborate with our mosques on this matter.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For example, MUIS has organised similar events in October 2020, by conducting a Fatwa Seminar on LPAs and Advanced Care Planning.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These should be encouraged. : Sir, in conclusion, I appreciate the general trend towards conducting business and legal transactions remotely.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe that, in the case of LPAs, we should go to where the people are.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I rise in support of the Electronic Conveyancing and Other Matters Bill.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I appreciate the objectives behind the introduction of DCP.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It streamlines the conveyancing process, enhances convenience and minimises the risk of clerical errors, issues that are often only discovered at the completion stage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Has SLA secured sufficient buy-in from all or if not, majority of the stakeholders, such as the real estate agents, property developers, banks that offer mortgage loans and law firms that provide conveyancing services?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If not, what are the reasons and how will they be addressed?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If no, a real concern could be that old habits die hard.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Without a mandated shift, certain stakeholders, such as banks and law firms, may be resistant to change their established workflows and standard operating procedures.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For instance, under current arrangements, deposits or conveyancing monies can be held in either: one, a law firm's conveyancing account; two, with the Singapore Academy of Law under its Conveyancing Money Service; or three, via DCP's Digital Conveyancing Account.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each of these options involve different workflows, timelines for deposits and procedures for releasing its funds.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To kickstart adoption of DCP, I suggest that the transactions involving Government agencies, such as HDB and the CPF Board, take the lead in using DCP.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Additionally, the Singapore Academy of Law could consider sunsetting its current escrow fee arrangements with a view to eventually merging them into the DCP framework.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also recommend that the SLA partner with institutions, like the Temasek Polytechnic's Diploma in Law and Management, Law Society of Singapore and Council of Estate Agencies, to organise workshops to train the relevant stakeholders, such as students, paralegals, lawyers and real estate agents, in DCP skills so that we can start developing a skilled workforce to support this transition.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Does this extend to Powers of Attorney for the sale, rental or general management of a real property?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, under section 48 of the Conveyancing and Law of Property Act (CLPA), the original Power of Attorney, engrossed with a seal, must be deposited with the High Court.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the virtual execution on PETS satisfy this requirement moving forward or will amendments to the CLPA be needed?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   SLA's DCP makes property transactions seamless, transparent and secure for buyers, sellers, lawyers and estate salespersons.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It enables the use of secure electronic systems for conveyancing, allows remote witnessing of legal instruments and introduces important reforms to facilitate digital signing of LPA.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These are practical, necessary changes, especially in a society that is increasingly digital in how we live, how we work and plan for the future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite years of digital progress, much of this process remains manual, paper-based and prone to coordination issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The amendments in this Bill provide a legal foundation for property transactions to be conducted fully through PETS.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These include systems, like DCP, which is developed by SLA.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This shift enables electronic contracts and deeds, secure digital signatures and the remote witnessing of execution.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that these capabilities are not just about efficiency.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They also reduce error, increase transparency and improve the overall experience for buyers, sellers and professionals involved.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Stakeholders have long highlighted inefficiencies, from repeated data entries to the delay in cheque processing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As our population continues to age, more individuals are planning ahead to safeguard their care and decision-making.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This builds on the earlier digitalisation of the LPA process through OPGO.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a meaningful reform that expands access, while preserving integrity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There are still segments of our population, particularly our seniors and our low-income families, who may lack digital access or confidence in the system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, we must ensure that no one is disadvantaged because they are unfamiliar with the new system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, not all conveyancing firms have equal digital capabilities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some smaller practices may face resource constraints in adopting new workflows.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will there be training or transition support provided for smaller law firms and service providers?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What measures will be taken to ensure that the new systems are inclusive, especially for residents who may struggle with digital tools or with the language?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But public confidence depends not just on what the law allows, but how risks are managed in practice.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, may I ask to that end, what cybersecurity standards will the prescribed systems be subjected to?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will there be regular system testing or independent audits that can be regularly done and how will the authorities communicate these safeguards to the public to build greater confidence?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When large sums and legally binding documents are involved, Singaporeans must know that the digital infrastructure is not just about convenience, but of course, trustworthy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Remote work, lockdowns and safe distancing rules revealed the limits of a manual, paper-dependent system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill ensures that critical legal and housing processes can continue securely, even when in-person meetings are not possible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a future-proofing measure which I welcome because it is not just a tech upgrade.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This move will enhance efficiency, security and convenience for all parties, including senior citizens and families who require additional support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is important that we ensure that in our journey towards digitalisation, no group is left behind.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes seniors, whom I mentioned earlier, and those who are not fluent in English.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I welcome this measure and hope that its implementation will be inclusive and build public confidence towards this system. : This Bill supports a more efficient, secure and accessible conveyancing system, and expands legal access for those planning for their future care.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As implementation begins, I urge the Government to continue working closely with stakeholders across the law, finance, tech and the community sector to ensure that this digital transition is smooth, inclusive and robust.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome this step in our continued journey to become a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new conveyancing portal makes our property transactions more efficient and further strengthens our place as a future-ready financial hub.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding my support, I have four points of clarifications.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As more of our Government interactions enter the digital space, it comes at a cost to our seniors.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Our seniors have gone through most of their lives without digital tools and now they find themselves in the midst of a rapid roll-out of new digital platforms in each part of their life.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I have strong faith in the ability of our seniors to adapt and learn.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But, I also worry that as the world becomes increasingly foreign, it can leave some feeling disempowered and disorganised.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially so for isolated seniors who do not have younger family members to help them.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: So, it is our responsibility to make the Smart Nation transition as easy as possible for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: For the new DCP, can the Minister clarify what parts of these new systems would be accessed by retail property owners?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Or would the platform be operated primarily by stakeholders, such as lawyers, bankers and property agents?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Are these public-facing user interfaces designed with our seniors in mind?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Support for multiple languages, visual impairment or simply good design thinking, this would go a long way in helping our seniors.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, digitalisation brings convenience and efficiency but also risks.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In the last few years, we have all experienced how the rise of digital banking services has led to an increase in scams, cheating some seniors out of their retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry assessed whether an electronic portal like this might increase the risks of scams, especially for our seniors?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Is it possible for a scammer or even a family member exerting undue influence over a senior to abuse the system?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Could the use of digital systems make it harder for stakeholders to detect when some improper conduct is taking place?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the Bill creates a new process for the remote witnessing of donors executing LPAs.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I agree, in principle, that for older Singaporeans, more safeguards may be appropriate before allowing remote witnessing, but the choice of 75 years appears a little arbitrary.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State explain how the age of 75 was chosen?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Could this be interpreted as a general rule that those above 75 have a higher risk of reduced mental capacity?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will this number be constantly and regularly reviewed as ageing trends in our society change?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, this Bill is a missed opportunity to go further and clarify other formalities and technical terms around executing legal documents in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: For example, this Bill allows deeds, which have specific legal requirements, to be executed electronically.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But why not abolish the concept of a deed entirely?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The difference between a deed and an agreement is a technical one that only lawyers are concerned with.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: There is some uncertainty whether a deed can be enforceable if it is not in wet ink or missing a red sticker.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These are old practices that carry little meaning to those signing them, but also increases business costs.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: So, as we become a Smart Nation, Sir, we can boldly abolish dated technical legal instruments and replace them with more intuitive processes that are more consistent with what we do in our modern world.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I am concerned about the impact on our elderly after the amendments.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Are these public-facing user interfaces designed with our seniors in mind?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Support for multiple languages, visual impairment, or simply good design thinking, would go a long way to helping our seniors.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, whilst digitalisation brings convenience, it also brings risks.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We all know the threat that scams pose to the public, especially to the elderly.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, one of the conditions is that the donor must be under 75 years old.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I understand this may be an additional safeguard for older individuals, but I would like to know how the age of 75 was determined.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will it be adjusted in future based on changing social circumstances? : Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill moves us in this direction and I hope to see the Government continuing on this momentum.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will make property transactions faster, more transparent and more efficient, in line with our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet as we digitalise, we must remember that buying or selling a home is not just a legal exchange.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a deeply human experience, a lifelong dream for some and an essential lifeline for others.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we move this process online, we must ensure it remains safe, inclusive and trustworthy for all, from young couples buying their first Build-To-Order flats to retirees unlocking equity in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have seen how initiatives, like Singpass and LifeSG, have set a new standard for convenience for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, we also know that not everyone is equally comfortable navigating digital platforms, particularly our seniors and small firms still reliant on paper-based workflows.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that no one gets left behind?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider assisted digital services at community touchpoints, such as libraries, community clubs and ServiceSG centres, where residents can receive guided in-person help from trained officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such digital assistance can make the difference between empowerment and exclusion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, as many small law firms rely heavily on conveyancing work, can the Government share the onboarding and training programmes to help these firms transition smoothly to the new system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will not only safeguard livelihoods but also preserve healthy competition in the legal sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the portal faces downtime on a critical completion day, what manual fallback or contingency processes will protect users from financial losses or penalties?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My second point, Mr Speaker, Sir, concerns remote witnessing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may inadvertently exclude Singaporeans who are temporarily based overseas, for instance, those on overseas postings or students abroad.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry explore secure extensions, perhaps through our embassies, consulates or accredited notaries, so that they, too, can safely participate?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, for residents who lack access to devices or who are not digitally confident, can we set up assisted witnessing stations at community hubs or HDB branches, equipped with secure connectivity and trained staff?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most importantly, the rules governing remote witnessing should be designed with compassion and flexibility, accommodating medical or disability-related circumstances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because for a hospitalised senior or a person with limited mobility, accessibility is not a convenience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, I note that there have been instances where lawyers in property transactions falsely certified documents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One example is the case of Ms K Manickam, who attested that she had witnessed several signings even though the documents had not been signed in her presence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the electronic system be able to ensure that individuals who are required to attest to the validity or correctness of documents do in fact fulfill this duty?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, electronic systems may create the false impression that digital transactions are somehow less formal or serious.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there measures in place to ensure that all parties and stakeholders understand the gravity of these transactions and that, despite the electronic system, the expectation remains that everyone involved is accountable for the verifications set out in the relevant documents?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even the most secure systems can experience glitches or cyber incidents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But for residents, especially families in the midst of completing a purchase, a few hours' delay can translate into real stress and financial penalties, especially when tax deadlines or stamp duties are triggered.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, when a transaction fails due to no fault of the user, who bears the cost?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be an ex-gratia or compensation framework for affected parties, particularly home buyers who may face cascading penalties through no fault of their own?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, will SLA publish audit trails or digital transaction logs so that parties can easily verify what went wrong and when?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As digital conveyancing scales up, what redundancy capabilities will ensure that the system can handle peak volumes, for example, after policy announcements that trigger surges in property transactions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My fifth point, Mr Speaker, Sir, is on data privacy and scam protection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe Members earlier, like Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Lee Hui Ying, have raised similar issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Property transactions involve highly sensitive financial and personal information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill allows SLA and HDB to provide non-confidential data for transparency and analytics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can certainly enhance policy planning and public understanding of market trends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify what data use limits and access safeguards will be in place to prevent misuse, such as bulk scraping or phishing attempts?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, will any of the data in this portal be used to fight crime?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What jurisdiction will be extended to the use of data in this portal without a resident's permission for criminal investigation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I also urge the Ministry to anticipate the evolving threat landscape, including deepfake impersonations in remote witnessing and phishing attempts masquerading as official DCP communications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given recent public sector data breaches, security assurance must be visible and continual, not just technical but also educational.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents must know how to verify authentic communication from the system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Physical title deeds may soon become a relic of the past.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But digital records raise a new set of questions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure permanence, authenticity and accessibility across generations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But for many residents, property ownership extends decades beyond any prescribed timeline.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But let us also remember what this Bill truly represents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not just about faster processing or cleaner interfaces.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about people, ensuring that every Singaporean, young or old, rich or poor, feels confident and included in this new digital journey.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must build a system that is inclusive so that no senior or small firm is left behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must make it compassionate, with remote witnessing that understands the realities of caregiving, disability and distance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must keep it accountable so that when things go wrong, there is redress, transparency and fairness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure it is secure because in a world of rising scams and cyber threats, trust is our strongest currency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must make it enduring so that the records of one generation remain safe in the hands of the next.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we can do all these, then this Bill will be more than just a technical milestone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will say that in Singapore, even as we digitalise, we do not lose our human touch.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We use technology to lift people up, not to leave them behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We build systems that are efficient, yes, but also empathetic, transparent and just.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is built on trust, on the faith that when we click that button, sign that document or buy that first home, the system will stand by our side.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, let us build this new chapter of our Smart Nation with courage and care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us create not only a faster system, but a fairer one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not just a connected nation, but a confident people.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Above all, let us remember: a truly smart nation is not defined by how many systems we build, but by how deeply we keep faith with the people they are meant to serve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I am heartened by the positive reception to the proposed expansion of remote witnessing to more donors in the making of the LPA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many users have found the online LPA application process convenient and user-friendly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To Dr Wan Rizal's concern that there are segments of our population who may lack digital access or confidence, we fully empathise and will continue with community partners and ServiceSG Centres to provide the necessary support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Anyone can still visit a Certificate Issuer to do an in-person witnessing and n fact, we fully expect that some donors may still prefer to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying asked how we decided on the age criterion of 75 years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: MSF will continue to monitor trends and if needed, propose adjustments to the age criterion to ensure its relevance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi asked about how the Public Guardian would ensure that there are no significant risk of fraud or undue pressure on the donor in the LPA making process, and that the donee will not act in the best interest of the donor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Before donors can have the LPA's witness remotely, the Public Guardian must assess and approve only donors who meet the legislated criteria.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These prescribed criteria ensure that donors with lower risk applications are eligible for remote witnessing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On top of the age criterion raised by Ms Lee Hui Ying, remote witnessing is only extended to donors who intend to appoint donees who are family members or professional deputies and licensed trust companies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This is because family members are likely to act in the best interest of the donor and in addition, professional deputies and licensed trust companies are regulated, so there is a lower risk that they will abuse or exploit the donor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Fadli Fawzi earlier raised concerns about LPA related disputes involving family members.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Most disputes involve family members, because most appointed donees today are family members of the donor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The whistle-blowing reports received by the OPG tend to come from other family members of the donor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We would like to underscore that, besides reviewing whether the donor's application meets the legislated criteria, the Public Guardian will also factor in other available information, such as the donor's history and past interactions with the OPG, as well as concerns raised by relevant individuals that may suggest that the donor is at risk of fraud or undue pressure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: During the LPA certification process, be it through in-person or remote witnessing, the Certificate Issuers play a critical role as gatekeepers of risk.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At the point of LPA execution, Certificate Issuers verify that: one, no fraud or undue pressure was used to induce the donor to create the LPA; two, the donor understands the purpose of the instrument; and three, there is nothing else that would prevent an LPA from being created by the instrument.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Certificate Issuers must also be satisfied that during the session the donor is executing the instrument in private by requiring the donor to pan the camera around the room to show that there is no third party present and if the Certificate Issuer assesses that the donor may be vulnerable to fraud or undue pressure, the Certificate Issuer has the full discretion to require an in-person witnessing or to refuse to certify the LPA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In addition, we have put in place administrative safeguards, such as having the Certificate Issuers document and submit to OPG records of the certification process, including the reason for any third party's presence and the identity of the third party in their notes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And this includes how they have assessed that the donor understands the purpose of an LPA and the scope of authority conferred under it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We will also provide training to prepare to prepare Certificate Issuers for remote witnessing, so that they are fully equipped to offer this option.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi also asked whether we could reach out to ethnic minority groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Collaterals, such as those titled "Guides to the Lasting Power of Attorney", "LPA quick reference guides", for instance, are already made available in vernacular languages and there are also various LPA awareness workshops which are being conducted in vernacular languages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our collaboration with various community partners, including the Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS), has thus far been positive and we will continue to work with them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked about cybersecurity standards that the prescribed systems will be subject to, as well as if there will be regular system testing or independent audits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The OPGO system used for online LPA applications is hosted on the Government commercial cloud, which has inbuilt cybersecurity measures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We would like to assure the Member that the system complies with the Government's cybersecurity and data protection standards, and there are also regular security audits, including penetration testing and vulnerability assessments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi asked about the anticipated take-up rate for remote witnessing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Members have raised questions on three main areas in relation to the DCP and the proposed conveyancing-related amendments: first, ensuring effective user adoption of the DCP through training and engagement; second, the security and integrity of the digital system; and third, the safeguards available to ensure accountability and protection against fraud and scams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Members have also raised various general clarifications such as the scope of the legislative amendments and the implementation approach for digital conveyancing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member Ms Hany Soh asked whether SLA has secured buy-in from stakeholders such as banks, law firms and real estate agents while the hon Members Mr Yip Hon Weng and Dr Wan Rizal asked about onboarding and training programmes to help law firms transition smoothly to the new system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP was designed with extensive input from stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We recognise that stakeholders will need time to adapt to the new system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Training and support will be provided to practitioners to facilitate a smooth transition.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, SLA is conducting industry briefings, training sessions and preparing user guides to help lawyers and conveyancing professionals navigate the DCP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: SLA will continue with their extensive engagement efforts to ensure a smooth transition.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hon Members Mr Yip, Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Lee Hui Ying asked about the measures that will be taken to ensure that the DCP is inclusive, especially for residents who may struggle with digital tools.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip and Dr Wan Rizal suggested having assisted digital services and witnessing stations at community touchpoints and help channels for residents who require help on the use of DCP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ms Lee also suggested that the DCP incorporate support for multiple languages and visual impairment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We will continue to work with all stakeholders in the design and implementation of the DCP to bridge the digital gap and ensure that the DCP is user-friendly to all users, including seniors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For instance, SLA had in fact considered visually impaired users and designed the DCP with mobile responsiveness and support for extra-large fonts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Lawyers will also continue to represent and assist buyers and sellers through the conveyancing process when the DCP is implemented.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Members have also raised the issue of DCP adoption and the cost of using the system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hon Members Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Soh had asked whether the DCP is intended to eventually be the only platform for conveyancing, while Mr Nair suggested signalling to the market to encourage more people to transact electronically during the transition process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ms Soh also suggested mandating transactions involving Government agencies, such as HDB, CPF Board to kickstart the adoption of the DCP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip asked if fees will be charged for using the DCP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I explained in my speech earlier, the DCP is developed in phases, with a view to eventually covering all property transactions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This measured approach will allow stakeholders to adapt to new digital conveyancing workflows progressively and enables SLA to incorporate practitioner feedback and refine workflows at each stage, resulting in a more robust and user-friendly system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But this will have to be reviewed once the DCP is fully implemented as there will be a cost to providing the new service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: When agencies review the fees that needs to be introduced in future, they will consider the benefits that the system brings to users as well as the overall affordability and accessibility of the system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip asked whether the electronic system would be able to ensure that individuals, like lawyers, who are required to attest to the validity or correctness of documents do, in fact, fulfil this duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He also asked whether there are measures in place to ensure that all parties and stakeholders understand the gravity of the transactions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To address this, the DCP has been designed to include clear warnings and confirmations at critical stages, requiring users to acknowledge the legal implications of their actions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: SLA’s training programmes for legal professionals have also emphasised that electronic transactions carry the same legal weight and professional responsibilities as traditional processes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip, Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Soh asked about cybersecurity standards that the DCP is subject to and whether there are safeguards in place to prevent misuse, such as bulk scraping and phishing attempts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Dr Wan Rizal also asked whether there will be regular system testing or independent audits.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP will operate on the Government Cloud Infrastructure and adopt security controls and processes in accordance with Government cybersecurity guidelines and best practices.
