speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Regular security audits and penetration testing will be conducted to maintain system resilience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP incorporates robust access controls to ensure information remains confidential and is only available to transaction parties, legal representatives and relevant authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The data will be used for better policy decisions and market analysis while ensuring that genuinely confidential information, such as personal financial details or private correspondence, remains protected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To Mr Yip's question on what jurisdiction will be extended to the use of data in the portal without a resident's permission for criminal investigation, data in the DCP may be subject to existing legal frameworks that govern law enforcement access to information.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Any use of portal data for criminal investigations would follow established legal procedures, including appropriate warrants or court orders where required.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ms Lee asked whether the DCP might increase the risks of scams and whether there is a possibility of family members exerting undue influence over a senior to abuse the system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, secure log in and secure electronic signing via Singpass or CorpPass will protect sensitive information and reduce the risk of fraud.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In addition, lawyers must continue to ensure that their clients are not under undue influence from other persons when signing DCP documents using Singpass.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip asked whether there are any manual fallback or contingency processes in the event the DCP faces downtime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP is designed to ensure a high level of availability of services and includes mechanisms for data replication and failover to prevent data loss.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the unlikely event the DCP is unavailable, users may continue with their transactions using the current manual process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: SLA will implement a business continuity management plan to enable online transactions to be completed offline quickly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip asked for assurance that digital conveyancing records will be archived indefinitely and remain accessible to homeowners or their legal representatives, even after technology platforms evolve or vendors change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP will maintain all digital records and provide homeowners with access to download their documents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Any such changes would be implemented with appropriate notice and clear guidelines about what constitutes chargeable versus free access.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Nair raised the issue of mistakes in the electronic forms and suggested for the DCP to provide flexibility for such transactions to be upheld, similar to the current paper-based system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP mirrors today's conveyancing process, particularly, during critical milestones in the transaction, such as the exercise of the Option.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There should be thus similar flexibility under the DCP in the event of any mistakes in the form.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The DCP is also linked to SLA's Singapore Titles Automated Registration System (STARS), which enables access to information in the Land Register.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip asked whether it is possible to explore secure extensions, for example, through our embassies, consulates or accredited notaries, to allow Singaporeans who are temporarily based overseas to engage in remote witnessing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As not all jurisdictions currently have similar laws allowing for remote witnessing of the execution of documents, both signatories and witnesses have to be in Singapore, so as to maintain legal certainty and avoid potential conflicts with any foreign law requirement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ms Soh asked whether the new section 16W of the Bill will allow deeds relating to immovable property to be executed virtually and whether it extends to Powers of Attorney related to property matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ms Lee also spoke about reforming the law on deeds generally, including the abolishment of the deeds' regime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Most common law jurisdictions still require a deed to be entered in many transactions and these must comply with the common law formalities for the execution of deeds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Similarly in Singapore, deeds apply in various aspects of our commercial activities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Other than real estate transactions, parties execute deeds in many contractual and non-contractual or legal arrangements.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, an agreement, not for valuable consideration, is not enforceable unless in the form of a deed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Other examples include trust deeds, deeds of guarantees and deed polls.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The formalities required for the execution of a deed also raises the signature level of the documentation to the parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Abolishing the use of the deeds may thus increase the incidence of fraud and affect how businesses deal with those from other countries on the common law system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The current amendments only enable deeds to be electronically executed on the DCP if they are required as part of the conveyancing journey.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Government is studying the feasibility of enacting legislative frameworks that will facilitate electronic executions of other instruments, including deeds.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for the Senior Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: I understand that Certificate Issuers must keep records of donors making LPAs, and this must be furnished as needed in the event of a dispute.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary confirm whether the remote witnessing sessions must be recorded or does it only involve a written report?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: OPG actually will provide the Certificate Issuers with a standardised template for LPA certification.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: As part of this template, Certificate Issuers must document how they have assessed that the donor understands the purpose of the instrument, as well as the scope of authority that is conferred under this instrument, and that no fraud or undue pressure was used to induce the donor to create this LPA.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: First, I must declare that I am a practising lawyer in family law, who volunteers in the Law Society's Probate Practice Committee.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The first question is pertaining to the Certificate Issuer playing a critical role, to ensure that the donor signs the LPA without duress and in this case, in a remote situation, I think on the point that the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has just mentioned about expecting written documentations and making sure that this whole process has taken place in a secured way without any duress, can I enquire, because at this point in time, I believe that the attendance notes that any Certificate Issuers would take may vary across between lawyers and doctors, and for example, the judges may feel that there is a higher expectation, from lawyers' point of view, to exercise extra caution and diligence in ensuring that the documents are signed without duress.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: So, may I suggest that whether MSF can consider issuing a guidance note unifying the expectations of Certificate Issuers, be it from the doctors or the lawyers, to make sure that we are all on the same page, and ensuring that a consistent standard of quality and services are being rendered to ensure and minimise the risk of any disputes that arise subsequently?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The second and third clarifications are on how we can help to increase the take-up rate of LPA.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I agree with the Senior Parliamentary Secretary and wish to commend the efforts that, over the years, community partners, for example, Pro Bono SG, the Community Development Councils have been rolling out in the community to organise law awareness talks, particularly targeting the minority groups as well, and we even have the Family Justice Courts rolling out community law awareness talks in the community as well over the years to increase such awareness.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: But at the same time, I can recognise that a lot of seniors, they understand that it is important to do a LPA, but perhaps this topic still remains as a morbid one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: And in terms of doing a comprehensive legacy planning or estate planning, they may think that perhaps they can prioritise in doing the nominations for CPF first, but try to delay on the doing of a LPA and doing of a will.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I can understand that over the years the Government has rolled out many initiatives, for example, the Legacy Portal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: So, my suggestion is whether we can consider how we try and increase awareness or encouragements of the take-up rate of doing a comprehensive estate planning in this aspect, which means encouraging more to sign up through the Legacy Portals, how the legacy portal can help to —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Soh, you might want to just get to your clarification and not make a speech.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: On Certificate Issuers, indeed, it is a critical role that they are playing.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: That is why we are phasing out the implementation.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: We are starting with a smaller group of Certificate Issuers, we are providing training, we are giving templates just to be sure that the standards of recording are consistent across the board.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: With regards to the second question, I think this is a case where sometimes the heart and the brain go in different directions.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: I fully understand that, but I guess, other than just increasing or re-designing the Legacy Portal, perhaps what might be most important would be to speak to the hearts of the potential target audience, which many of them are our seniors in the community, and what would they be caring about.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: I think they will be caring about their family members, their loved ones, especially when they themselves lose mental capacity, and therefore, their family members and loved ones' peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: And I think that is the biggest "sell" whenever we reach out to seniors, senior citizens in the community.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: That is, to pitch to them, that whatever they do actually adds to the peace of mind of their loved ones, and I think that is the key point that I would want to push across.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: On the third point, we are having a conversation with the Ministry of Finance and we will share more details when we have them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Murali, do you want to chime in?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I heard what Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua said just now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.00 pm until 3.20 pm.
